content.text: Mapster copies members whose names match, so it removes typing, not mapping bugs. By default, a destination member with no source keeps its default value, enums are copied by number, and mapping onto an existing object copies nulls, all without an error. The belief: a convention-based mapper like Mapster removes mapping bugs, because it maps matching properties automatically. No hand-written assignments means no forgotten lines and no

It's an easy belief to hold. Hand-written mapping really is where typos live, and a project with fifty DTOs has a lot of it that nobody reviews carefully. Mapster's README opens with "Writing mapping methods is a machine job", and for the simple case it's right: same names and types map correctly, and fast. The half-truth is that the typing goes away but the decisions don't. Which source feeds which member, and what a missing one means, are still decided, now by conventions at run time instead of by code the compiler reads.

blocks.title: Opinion: how we'd split the work

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from Mapster's docs. Use Mapster with strict mode for the read side, entity to DTO, where conventions save the most code and a compiled check catches drift. Write the write side, request to entity, by hand: it's short, it names exactly what a client may change, and it's where a wrong match does real damage.
